Chapter Five: The Six Kinds (Five Versions). Regarding the reason why this chapter appears:
the Buddha follows the various divergent explanations of deluded sentient beings.
Sometimes they employ the names of the five aggregates (skandhas),
and sometimes they designate the six categories;
yet their intent lies in the refutation of the self (ātman).
This causes me to see that even the dharma of cessation does not remain.
Those who cling to the teachings do not comprehend selflessness, but merely grasp at and become attached to dharmas.
Thus, the fifth delusion has been refuted.
Now, this chapter is taught again in order to eliminate six kinds of delusion.
Second, regarding the various Mahāyāna sūtras that expound the Dharma and open the path:
some contemplate the five aggregates as being the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Alternatively, by examining the six kinds [of dharmas], one is led to realize the Dharmakāya.
Now, desiring to provide a comprehensive explanation of all sutras and to exhaustively investigate all phenomena, this chapter is taught.
Third, the body of birth and death generally consists of two parts.
First is the portion of existence;
second is the portion of emptiness.
From the analysis of causes and conditions through to the five aggregates, one destroys that portion of existence.
This chapter refutes the division of emptiness,
causing one to realize that this body is fundamentally non-existent from the beginning;
yet it is not non-existent now either— this state of being neither existent nor non-existent is precisely the Middle Way.
This chapter is taught because one cultivates contemplation within the causal stage to sever all afflictions.
Fourth, the Sūtra states that "all phenomena are profoundly deep," which refers to the three gates of liberation.
The *Śata-śāstra* states: "If there were wisdom or vision apart from emptiness and signlessness, then the word 'emptiness' would be without reality.
The above has clarified the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*).
Now, the gate of signlessness (animitta-mukha) is explained.
If one enters through awakening by means of the gate of emptiness (śūnyatā), the gate of signlessness is not required;
however, if one grasps at the characteristic of emptiness itself, it is no longer a gate.
Now, this chapter refutes the characteristics of emptiness so that one may enter through the gate of signlessness and give rise to right contemplation;
therefore, this chapter exists.
Therefore, the reason why the characteristics of space were refuted at the beginning of this chapter is intended to convey this point.
Furthermore, all phenomena are of two kinds.
First is the internal essence;
second is the external characteristic.
Therefore, the sutras clarify emptiness of intrinsic nature and emptiness of specific characteristics.
The preceding clarified that there is no internal substance;
now it is distinguished that there are no external characteristics.
This is precisely the emptiness and quiescence of the nature and characteristics of all phenomena.

The purpose of clarifying that nature and characteristics are empty and quiescent is precisely to distinguish between the similarities and differences of the two types of emptiness in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
In the Hīnayāna, one analyzes nature and characteristics to clarify emptiness;
this is a teaching of arising and ceasing, serving as a contemplation of arising and ceasing.
The Mahāyāna clarifies that intrinsic nature is empty and specific characteristics are empty;
it elucidates the teaching of non-arising and non-ceasing and the contemplation of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Therefore, the treatise distinguishes the emptiness of nature and characteristics as being taught for those of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, it causes those of the Hīnayāna to turn away from the small vehicle and enter the Great Vehicle;
thus, it clarifies that nature and characteristics are fundamentally empty and quiescent,
as in the commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Those with craving and views enter through the gate of signlessness (*animitta-mukha*).
Craving is a venomous insect, and views are evil ghosts."
By what means can one be separated from them? One should contemplate signlessness (*animitta*).
When all objects are signless, the mind that grasps at signs does not arise;
craving and views are thereby severed, and one attains liberation from the three realms.
By contemplating signlessness through the destruction of signs, one immediately emerges from the realm of分段 (paricchinna-bhava).
By realizing that signs are fundamentally signless, one escapes the burning house of the three realms, both internal and external;
thus, all burdens are stilled and all virtues are perfected.
Fifth, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"The four great elements enclose space, and consciousness resides within them;
these are conventionally designated as a 'person'."
Emptiness is the root of the four great elements;
the four great elements are the root of consciousness;
and consciousness is the root of sentient beings.
From the beginning up to this point, we have refuted its branches;
now, in this chapter, we shall successively refute its root.
Because the branches are manifest, they were refuted first.
Because it was originally obscured, it is subsequently eliminated.
Sixth, from the preceding section onward, one cycle of refuting existence is completed.
The four conditions refer to the causes of the myriad dharmas.
The aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is the fruit of all phenomena.
Once those who have destroyed the delusions regarding cause and effect claim that there is neither cause nor fruit, and thus this is a discourse on emptiness like empty space.
For this reason, Nāgārjuna was called the "Bhikṣu of the Emptiness Discourse."
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* when exhorting the various brāhmaṇas to resolve upon bodhicitta:
"How can one cause people to be identical to space?
For they would then claim that space is non-existent."
The Mahāyāna is likewise.
Therefore, this present chapter refutes space.
Seventh, from the conclusion of the discussion on the past and future, the five aggregates refute the three conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
In this chapter, the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are next refuted so that both the conditioned and the unconditioned are ultimately empty. Therefore,
after the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), the ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) is explained.
Eighth, at the end of the "Chapter on the Five Aggregates," there is a dialogue exhorting outsiders to rely upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The outsider then grasps the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*);
therefore, this chapter follows by refuting [that misconception of] emptiness.
Ninth, many Mahāyāna sūtras frequently cite empty space as a metaphor.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"Prajñā is like empty space."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Buddha-nature is like space;
the Dharma-body of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is like space."
Many who are deluded do not recognize empty space;
they are thus confused regarding the dharma illustrated by this metaphor.
Now, I shall refute the false notion of empty space and set forth the correct understanding of empty space.
Therefore, this present chapter has come forth.
For now, let us clarify this by means of a single matter:
the Buddha’s body, his Dharma-body, is like empty space.
If one explains space as being permanent and all-pervasive,
it is the space of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
To take space as a metaphor for the Buddha’s Dharma-body is to equate the Dharma-body with that of the non-Buddhists.
If one takes the Abhidharma position that space is an existent phenomenon (*bhāva*),
then the Buddha-body in the Buddha-dharma would be the same as the Abhidharma body. If, however,
one follows the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) and holds that space is a non-existent phenomenon (*abhāva*).
This is precisely the fulfillment of the true Dharmakāya.
Since the metaphor is destroyed, the Dharma it expresses is likewise destroyed;
thus, all Mahāyāna sūtras would be rendered void.
This chapter refutes the erroneous [conception] of space and establishes the correct [conception] of space;
thus, all the teachings and analogies of the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras are rendered valid.
This is a matter of great significance.
You should deeply contemplate this.
Question: What are the similarities and differences between the six kinds of five aggregates (pañca-skandha)?
Answer: The five aggregates combine form (rūpa) and are separated from mind (citta).
The six types of mental application (manopavicāra) are dissociated from form (rūpa).
Furthermore, according to the Abhidharma doctrine, while the five aggregates (skandha) encompass both the out-flowing (sāsrava) and the non-out-flowing (anāsrava),
the six types of mental application are exclusively out-flowing.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*,
the five aggregates are proximate in their meaning of constituting a person,
whereas the six elements are remote in their meaning of constituting a person.
Just as the four atoms form the four great elements,
the four great elements form the five sense organs,
and the five sense organs form the aggregate of form.
The aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) constitutes sentient beings;
therefore, the four great elements (mahābhūta) are distant [to them], while the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are intimate.
Question: The Sāṃkhya school elucidates six categories (ṣaṭ-tattva); how do these compare in terms of their similarities and differences?
Answer: According to the Abhidharma, there are two kinds of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
First, the substantial dharma four great elements, which refers to the four tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*).
Second, the nominal four great elements, which refers to the formal appearances of earth and so forth.
In the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā), the categories of consciousness are exclusively contaminated (sāsrava);
in the Treatise on Establishment (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), they encompass both contaminated and uncontaminated (anāsrava).
Furthermore, the Abhidharma explains that space (ākāśa) is of two kinds.
The first is conditioned space (*saṃskṛta-ākāśa*),
such as the space within the bodies of sentient beings, or within wells, pits, doorways, and so forth.
The second is unconditioned space (*asaṃskṛta-ākāśa*).
It is that place where even birds cannot fly.
The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* clarifies that space (*ākāśa*) is a non-existent dharma;
it is merely unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Question: How are these six kinds to be contemplated?
Answer: As stated below, "Therefore, one knows that space is neither existent nor non-existent;
the same applies to the other five."
To realize that these six kinds [of phenomena] are neither existent nor non-existent is itself the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This gives rise to right contemplation (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), whereby all afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed,
and one no longer undergoes further existence in these six kinds of bodies.
Therefore, it is said that one contemplates these six categories.
Furthermore, if one perceives these six categories as either existent or non-existent,
then the body of birth and death will manifest while the Dharma-body will not.
That which manifests as the Dharma-body and accords with the Dharma-body is called the Response-body (Nirmāṇakāya).
Having attained realization in accordance with reality, one then expounds the truth for the sake of sentient beings in accordance with reality.
This is precisely the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Thus, the *Mañjuśrī-daśanāma-vidhi-sūtra* states:
"The Buddhas have the characteristic of space."
Space, too, is without marks;
because it is free from all causes and effects, I pay homage to that which is without an object of observation.
Thus, one should know that the observation of the six elements as neither existent nor non-existent is itself the Dharmakāya.
The arising of correct contemplation in correspondence with the Dharmakāya is called the Saṃbhogakāya;
teaching for the sake of sentient beings is the Nirmāṇakāya.
Furthermore, the three characters of the term *Madhyamaka-śāstra* are themselves the three bodies (*trikāya*).
The center is the Dharmakāya.
That which arises in correspondence with the center is the Sambhogakāya, which is right contemplation.
Contemplation is directed inward, while its expression manifests outwardly.
Therefore, the Treatise on Names is itself the Nirmāṇakāya.
This chapter is divided into two parts:
first, the establishment [of the position], and second, the refutation.
There are two [aspects] to its establishment:
first, clarifying its characteristics, and second, clarifying its essential nature.
Regarding the characteristic of stability, it is like the characteristic of solidity in earth, which cannot be made non-solid.
The characteristic of heat in fire cannot be made cold.
As for "there being six kinds":
since the characteristic exists, there must likewise exist the substantial entity (dharmatā).
This is the essential characteristic (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), not the indicative characteristic (*saṃjñā-lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, where there is a characteristic, there is necessarily an essence.
Question: What is the difference between the formulations in the preceding chapters and this formulation?
Answer: From the conditions and causes up to the five aggregates, the meaning of "existence" (bhāva) is established.
Now, the meaning of "establishing characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) is clarified.
Previously, because existence was established, the Master [Nāgārjuna] refuted existence to clarify emptiness as the gate of liberation.
Now, by establishing characteristics, one refutes characteristics to clarify the gate of liberation of signlessness;
this is the sequential order.
Within the response, the eight verses are divided into two parts.
The first seven verses constitute the gate of destroying characteristics to clarify signlessness (*animitta*).
The second single verse constitutes the gate of censure;
it clarifies non-existence according to the ultimate principle, thereby censuring those who, while [the truth is] non-existent, claim it to exist.
The first section also has two parts:
the preceding six verses refute space,
and the subsequent single verse applies this reasoning by analogy to the other five [elements].
The refutation of space is divided into two parts:
first, five and a half verses refute the nature of space;
next, half a verse refutes the person who knows space.
The first section has two parts:
the first five verses refute that space is existent;
the subsequent half-verse refutes that space is non-existent.
In the refutation of existence, there are five verses divided into four sections.
The first one and a half verses present the refuting characteristic as that which refutes the characterized;
the next one and a half verses present the characterized as that which refutes the refuting characteristic.
The third [section] consists of one verse that refutes [the notion of] characteristics and the characterized by means of their mutual dependence;
the fourth consists of one verse that concludes the refutation.
The first [section] of one and a half verses is divided into two parts.
The preceding verse constitutes the direct refutation;
the subsequent half-verse constitutes the indirect refutation.
The first half of the initial verse clarifies that if emptiness were dependent upon characteristics, it would fall into the error of being non-empty.
The second half clarifies that if emptiness does not depend on characteristics, it falls into the state of signlessness;
thus, one fails whether advancing or retreating.
The first half refutes this by stating: "As for your previous claim that each of the six elements possesses a fixed characteristic..."
If that were so, space would exist because its characteristics exist;
since its characteristics are absent,
space itself is non-existent.
Question: What is the characteristic of emptiness?
Answer: Emptiness has two kinds of characteristics:
first, the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Second, the characteristic of essence:
as when one perceives a pillar, upon knowing the pillar, there is immediately nothing external to it; because of the knowledge of existence, there is the knowledge of non-existence.
This is the defining characteristic of "non-existence" (abhāva).
Second, because the pillar is removed, the non-existence of the pillar is attained;
the state where the pillar is absent constitutes the essential characteristic of emptiness (śūnyatā).
However, these two characteristics both depend upon the pillar.
If this is so, then because the pillar exists, space can be apprehended;
if the pillar did not yet exist, space should likewise not yet exist.
Furthermore, space coexists with a pillar;
since the pillar is impermanent, space should likewise be so.
Question: The first half [of the verse] clarifies that where there are no characteristics, space is non-existent.
Is it non-existent through mutual dependence, or is it non-existent without mutual dependence?
Answer: It possesses both meanings.
If it is a characteristic of designation, it is non-existent because it exists only in dependence upon something else.
If it is a characteristic of essence, then if there is no characteristic, there is no essence either.
The second half [of the verse] refutes that phenomena do not coexist with characteristics.
If you say that space already exists before the pillar exists,
then space would be without characteristics. Yet,
you previously stated that each of the six elements possesses its own fixed characteristic.
This statement is erroneous.
Question: What characteristics does space lack?
Answer: Space exists even before any defining characteristics have appeared.
Therefore, this is merely the emptiness of signlessness.
If one says that there is no essence or characteristic,
then signlessness would be the same as non-emptiness.
Therefore, if there were no defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), one would fall into the error of losing the characteristic.
If there were no essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), there would be two errors: first, falling into the state of being without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*).
The second [point] is that falling into [the extreme of] non-existence lacks any substantiality. The prose commentary explains only the latter half [of the verse],
clarifying that falling into emptiness results in the signless (*animitta*).
The phrase "the non-existence of dharmas in the first half [of the verse]" is not explained until the second verse;
furthermore, since the absence of characteristics (*animitta*) is itself the non-existence of dharmas, this also serves as an explanation of the first half.
Question: The second half-verse below refutes the externalist’s claim that the six elements each possess a fixed characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
The externalist initially states that each of the six elements has a determinate characteristic.
Now, for what reason do you change your school of thought and claim that emptiness is a non-characterized existence?
Answer: The external teachings have both a fundamental and a derivative aspect.
According to the fundamental view, emptiness is an eternal dharma.
Since marks are impermanent,
emptiness already existed prior to the time when marks had not yet arisen;
therefore, emptiness is without marks.
Speaking from the perspective of the end, it is said that form subsequently arises.
Because one knows emptiness through the cessation of form, it is said that space has characteristics.
The initial statement regarding its having characteristics refers to its final state.
Now, the statement that "the signless is empty" refers to its fundamental nature;
therefore, these two assertions do not contradict one another.
The answer states that what follows refutes the notion that the signless is empty.
Regarding the statement "it does not exist in any place":
this clarifies that it is non-existent because it lacks an essential nature (*svabhāva*), not because it merely lacks a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
If it lacks an essential nature, then this thing does not exist at all.
There are two categories that encompass all phenomena:
first, conditioned phenomena; second, unconditioned phenomena.
Conditioned phenomena are characterized by arising, abiding, and ceasing.
The two unconditioned dharmas have non-arising, non-abiding, and non-ceasing as their characteristics.
Since these two each possess their own characteristics,
they are therefore existent dharmas.
If space were without characteristics, it would be neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
it would simply not exist as a phenomenon.
Therefore, it is said that it does not exist anywhere.
What is space? It is one among the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
How could it not be both conditioned and unconditioned?
Furthermore, according to the Abhidharma, there is both conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) and unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
Now, that which is neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is no dharma;
therefore, it is said that "it does not exist in any place.
The second half [of the verse] belongs to the second section, consisting of one and a half verses.
This cites the characterized (lakṣya) to refute the characterizer (lakṣaṇa),
further opening it into two distinct parts.
The first half-verse clarifies that because there is no characterized object, what could the characterizer characterize?
Next, one verse opens two gates to re-examine the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).
The first half-verse contains two intentions.
The first is to rescue the meaning of the first half by adopting its underlying intent.
If emptiness were ultimately without any characteristics to be apprehended and were a non-existent dharma,
then although it was previously without characteristics, characteristics would later come to characterize it;
therefore, it would possess characteristics.
Because there is a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), there is consequently a dharma.
Now, even if we were to refute this:
if there was no characteristic previously, how could a subsequent characteristic come to characterize it?
One ultimately does not cling to marks.
As it is commonly said:
"In ultimate truth, there are no names."
To designate the Real with names only serves to distance one further from the Real.
The second point states:
if there were no characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) from the outset, then there would be no phenomena (*dharma*) at all.
What does a subsequent characteristic characterize?
For example, a pillar has roundness as its characteristic;
if there were no characteristic of roundness, there would be no pillar.
What is its characteristic?
Space has formlessness as its characteristic.
If there were no formlessness, there would be no space.
What is the characteristic?
If one considers that there was previously no characteristic, the following explanation of the second half of the verse gives rise to the third stanza.

Regarding "having characteristics" and "lacking characteristics," the middle and lower sections [of this commentary] specifically refute the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) to explain the second half of the preceding verse.
The first half clarifies that the characteristics of both the existent and non-existent gates are unobtainable.
Regarding the method of subsumption in the latter half:
within the characteristics of existence, the non-abiding of characteristics has two meanings.
First, there are characteristics that have existed from the very beginning.
There is no further need for a characteristic;
it is like a pillar that already possesses a circular shape—
one does not require a further circular characteristic to characterize the pillar.
Second, if a circle already exists inherently and yet another circle must still be added,
then a single pillar would possess two circles,
and a single space would possess two marks.
If one pillar has two circles, it may likewise have one circle and two pillars;
furthermore, since there are already two characteristics,
there must be a third, and so on ad infinitum.
Regarding the fact that signs do not abide within signlessness, there are two meanings.
First, since the fundamental nature is already signless, even if one brings signs forward to characterize it,
they ultimately fail to adhere.
Second, if one takes formlessness alone as the essence of emptiness,
then since the characteristic of formlessness does not exist,
there would be no essence of emptiness.
"The subsequent characteristic has nothing for it to characterize.
The meaning of this verse is profound and its words far-reaching;
it clarifies that both conditioned and unconditioned dharmas are subject to this same critique.
All sentient beings alike maintain that the conditioned and the unconditioned each possess their own characteristics;
thus they give rise to a mind that grasps at characteristics.
This mind that grasps at characteristics is the very root of affliction.
Consequently, afflictions arise;
because of afflictions, there is karma and suffering.
Now, it is asserted that neither conditioned nor unconditioned characteristics can be apprehended.
Because there are no signs whatsoever,
one does not give rise to a mind that grasps at signs and thereby attains liberation.
The prose commentary explains the first half-verse in four parts.
First, the non-abiding of characteristics within the signless is explained;
next, the non-abiding of characteristics within the sign-possessing is explained;
finally, the non-abiding of characteristics within the signless is explained once more.
The fourth section.
In the verse, it was first explained that that which possesses marks does not abide;
now, the two meanings of that which is markless shall first be explained.
First, it is the fundamental tenet of the opponent's own school;
they establish that there was originally no characteristic, and subsequently, a characteristic comes and characterizes it.
Second, it is for the purpose of establishing the preceding verse.
One takes the horned peak itself as the body of the ox;
if this characteristic were absent, there would be no ox to be characterized.
Next, [the text] explains that within the "possessor of characteristics," the characteristic does not abide.
The mention of water and fire refers to first refuting sentient beings and now refuting non-sentient beings;
this is merely a reciprocal illustration.
Furthermore, the subsequent section provides a profound refutation of the fact that within the signless, signs do not abide.
First the absence of cause is indicated, and next the absence of cause is explained.
As for the statement that "there are characteristics despite the absence of dharmas": since it is said that there are no characteristics, there is nothing to be characterized.
The characterized (lakṣya) is the cause of the characterizer (lakṣaṇa).

Regarding the statement that "the characterizer and the characterized are always mutually dependent," the former [passage] clarified the absence of the characterized, while this [passage] clarifies the absence of the characterizer.
Because there is no dharma with characteristics that can be apprehended, there is no characteristicizer.
Therefore, the fourth verse below is cited as a conclusion:
"Because the dharma of characteristics does not exist."
This fourth verse refutes the relationship between the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) through their mutual dependence.
The first half clarifies that because the characteristic—which exists in dependence—is itself non-existent, the characterized is likewise non-existent.
The second half [clarifies] the dependence of the characteristic upon the characterized.
Because the characteristic (*lakṣya*) does not exist, the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is itself non-existent.
This also clarifies that the substance (*tattva*) and the characteristic are mutually dependent; since the substance and the characteristic do not exist, the characteristic is itself non-existent.
Second, if one applies the refutation of mutual dependence by means of the designated characteristic (*abhidheya-lakṣaṇa*):
The first three verses are called "refutation by individual analysis," while this present verse is called "refutation by mutual interconnection.
Regarding the clarification of the refutation by individual analysis in the preceding three verses:
The first two verses correctly refute the characterized (lakṣya);
the next single verse correctly refutes the characterizer (lakṣaṇa);
now this present verse refutes both the characterizer and the characterized together.
Therefore, it is called "interlacing.
Question: Previously, you refuted the characterizable (*lakṣya*) and subsequently refuted the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Why is it that now, first, you clarify that because the characteristic does not exist, the characterizable does not exist?
The subsequent explanation clarifies that because the characterizable (*lakṣya*) does not exist, the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) does not exist.
The response states: "This is a refutation by pursuing the immediate force [of the opponent's argument];
the third verse provides the formal refutation of the characteristic."
Therefore, by riding on the momentum of the destruction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), one immediately destroys that which possesses characteristics (*lakṣya*).
In the second half [of the verse], by riding on the first half to destroy that which possesses characteristics, one further destroys the characteristics themselves.
Thus, there is now no characteristic.
The fifth [point], the refutation of the method of summary, is as follows:
the first half summarizes what preceded, while the second half summarizes the dharma;
therefore, it is now without characteristics (*animitta*).
This concludes the second half of the fourth verse.
Furthermore, there is no characteristic to be defined;
this concludes the first half of the fourth verse.
Because these arise through mutual interlocking like a chain, they proceed from the bottom upward.
Regarding the summary of the phenomena of the lower half:
since the refutation of both characteristics and the characterized has been completed above, [the summary follows].
Now, since characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) encompass all phenomena (*dharma*),
and no phenomenon exists outside of essence, characteristics, the characterized, the indicator (*liṅga*),
and that which is indicated (*liṅgin*): since characteristics and the characterized do not exist, all phenomena are likewise non-existent.
The Long Discourse states:
Regarding the beginning and end of causes and conditions,
some say that because there are causal characteristics (*nimitta*), there are the characterized (*lakṣya*).
Because that which is characterized exists by virtue of its characteristics, it is called a "causal condition" (hetu-pratyaya).
That which is characterized is the root, while the characteristics are the branches.
Therefore, they are called "root and branch.
Furthermore, because they are mutually dependent, they serve as both root and branch to one another.
Now, what we call "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) is a term for the underlying reason.
"Root and branch" refers to the terminology for beginning and end.
By seeking this characteristic and that which is characterized through the beginning and end of a single chapter, neither can ultimately be found.
As for smoke also having a characteristic:
By day, fire is the signable and smoke is the sign;
by night, smoke is the signable and fire is the sign.
There are two meanings to this statement.
First, it is shown that the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) are not fixed;
second, it is shown that the characteristic and the characterized encompass all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
Question: If existence does not exist, then non-existence (*abhāva*) ought to exist.
From the preceding five verses, the refutation that space is existent is concluded.
Now, the second [section] refutes that space is non-existent.
This inquiry contains four points.
First, previously the Abhidharma and non-Buddhist schools were refuted for asserting that space is existent;
now the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* is refuted for asserting that space is non-existent.
The *Satyasiddhi* clarifies that space is a non-entity (*abhāva*).
Nevertheless, this dharma ultimately exists.

Question: What are the three characteristics?
Answer: The Sarvāstivādins say: [as follows].
Apart from the essence of phenomena (dharmatā), there are three distinct characteristics;
therefore, the essence of phenomena pervades all three aggregates,
while the three characteristics are neither form nor mind.
It is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). The *Tattvasiddhi*, the *Mahāsāṃghika*,
and other texts state that apart from the essence of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva*), there are no separate characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
That is to say, the arising of a dharma is called "birth" (jāti), its remaining is called "abiding" (sthiti), and its passing away is termed "cessation" (nirodha).
Question: Are these three characteristics conditioned (saṃskṛta) or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)?
The Sāṃkhyas likewise state:
"The three characteristics are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). The Vībhajyavādins say:
Conditioned phenomena do not possess inherent stability in their own essence;
how then could they influence others?
Yet, they are indeed able to influence others.
One should know that these three characteristics are unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*),
just as space can give rise to all transformations.
Next, Dharmagupta said:
The two characteristics of arising and abiding are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*),
while the characteristic of cessation is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛtadharma*); therefore, the three characteristics are both conditioned and unconditioned.
Question: Do the three characteristics arise simultaneously, or do they occur sequentially?
Answer: The Dārṣṭāntika school says:

Therefore, the three characteristics exist sequentially.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"The three conditioned phenomena all exist in the present."
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states:

The Abhidharma states:
"The essence and its function are simultaneous, yet their manifestation has a temporal sequence;

When a dharma exists in the future, its characteristic is also future;
when a dharma arises in the present, its characteristic is also present;
when a dharma passes away in the past, its characteristic likewise passes away.
Therefore, conditioned phenomena must necessarily coexist with their characteristics.
Thus it is said that while the essence arises simultaneously [with its characteristics], at the time the activity of arising occurs, the activity of abiding has not yet arisen;

Therefore, it is used according to what precedes and follows.

Question: For what reason are the three characteristics refuted?

First, regarding those who cling to the three characteristics:
Most are of the Hīnayāna;

Now, because he causes them to believe that all phenomena are empty, he refutes the three marks. Second,

However, they do not know that the intrinsic nature of the three characteristics is empty.
Now, in order to lead them to believe that the intrinsic nature of the three characteristics is itself empty,

Third, regarding the three characteristics (trilakṣaṇa) produced by the great and small, internal and external schools, their mutual refutations result in the failure of their own positions.
Herein, we shall now reveal the nature of this failure.
Therefore, it is said that [the opponent] is refuted.
It is the proponent who establishes the characteristics who refutes himself;

Those who maintain that there is no distinct entity refute the existence of a distinct entity;

Fourth, those of the Small Vehicle who hold to attainment are called followers of the "half-character" teaching.

As it was said when [the Buddha] rebuked Kātyāyana:

Non-arising and non-ceasing is the meaning of impermanence."
The Buddha taught impermanence (*anitya*) in order to refute permanence;

Therefore, non-arising and non-ceasing is the true meaning of impermanence.
Question: The Buddha taught that impermanence (anitya) refutes permanence.
Furthermore, he abandoned the notion of impermanence as arising and ceasing.
Why, then, do you now specifically state that non-arising and non-ceasing is the meaning of impermanence?
The answer is: Kātyāyana already knows that there is no permanence, yet he has not yet realized that there is no arising and ceasing, which is impermanence.

Nāgārjuna’s refutation of outsiders is no different from Vimalakīrti’s rebuke of Candra-kauṇḍinya.
Furthermore, the various schools commit two kinds of errors.

As for the statement that there are three, this is a teaching of three where there are actually no three;
the intent behind teaching the three lies in the absence of three.
This immediately gives rise to two kinds of wisdom and leads one into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The general intent regarding the appearance of Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions in the world is thus;
the general intent regarding the appearance of the four reliances (*catvāraḥ pratisaraṇāni*) in the world is likewise.
For this reason, various gates are opened to dismantle the three marks (*trilakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, those who cling to the existence of the three characteristics are mostly followers of the Hīnayāna.
Upon hearing the teaching of the three activities, they form three interpretations.
Now, the three activities are refuted to show that the three characteristics do not exist.
Because the three marks do not exist, the conditioned does not exist;
because the conditioned does not exist, the unconditioned also does not exist.
That all phenomena are ultimately empty is the sphere of the Buddha’s activity.
It causes followers of the Hīnayāna to turn away from the small toward the great, awakening to the ultimate emptiness of the three marks and attaining true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
They then realize that the Buddha’s former teaching of the existence of the three marks within the Hīnayāna was a skillful means (*upāya*) through which he attained provisional wisdom (*prajñā*).
This means being fully endowed with the skillful means that reveal the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"In the past, it was taught that the five aggregates are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing."
Now, in explaining the portion concerning the five aggregates as being neither permanent nor impermanent,
the sūtras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna directly proclaim them to be neither permanent nor impermanent;
those of sharp faculties then awaken to and study this immediately.
Those of dull faculties among the followers of the Mahāyāna have not yet understood this;
it shall now be explained in detail.
One who seeks the three characteristics of the conditioned cannot find them, and thus they are not impermanent.
Because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is also non-existent,
it is not eternal; this causes beginner bodhisattvas to realize and understand that the Mahāyāna is neither eternal nor impermanent,
so that they may recognize the Middle Way and give rise to right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).
Therefore, the three characteristics are refuted.
*Madhyamaka-śāstra-vṛtti*, Fascicle Five, Part One.
